<reason>Side B (PRO) built the stronger path to victory by maintaining a consistent distinction between measurable position/crossing calls and interpretive judgment calls, effectively rebutting the "procedural nightmare" charge by framing semi-automation as reducing discretion through defined triggers rather than adding litigation. Side B answered pressure questions directly with the required A1/A2 format and crystallized a compelling "bounded, auditable uncertainty" framework that contrasted favorably with human officiating's "unacknowledged uncertainty." Side A (CON) raised valid concerns about calibration variance and the interpretive nature of offside, but their final rebuttal was clipped for exceeding the word limit, and they repeated arguments without fully neutralizing Side B's core comparison regarding auditable error profiles.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's Rebuttal 2 (A1/A2) decisively answering the pressure questions by specifying that officials retain final authority only for protocol-defined malfunctions (not preference), and that calibration is standardized by league certification, establishing that the system reports "indeterminate" rather than manufacturing false precision when confidence intervals straddle the line—effectively neutralizing Side A's authority and calibration challenges.</best_rebuttal>
